passage:
Tuesday: Joseph saved the swing next to his for Reena, like always. She came late, breathless, talking about her new dance class and a girl called Mitali. She stayed five minutes, then ran to the steps where Mitali was waiting.
Friday: Reena didn't come to the swings at all. Joseph kicked the gravel and went over everything. Was it because he'd laughed when she fell in the relay race? Because his tiffin smelled of fish? He couldn't find the thing he did.
The next Wednesday: At home, he told his mother, "Reena doesn't like me any more."
Amma asked, "Did she say that?"
He thought about it. She hadn't. She'd just been busy, rushing off to dance practice twice a week with Mitali. Somehow that felt a little better, and still a bit sad.

qa.q: What did Joseph save for Reena on Tuesday?
qa.a: Joseph saved the swing next to his for Reena.

qa.q: What was Joseph worried about as he went over everything on Friday?
qa.a: Joseph worried he had done something wrong to make Reena leave, like laughing when she fell in the relay or his tiffin smelling of fish. 😔

qa.q: What helped Joseph at this stage, and what else could he try?
qa.a: Amma's question helped Joseph see that Reena never said she disliked him; next he could ask Reena to the swings on a day without dance practice.

qa.q: What might Reena be experiencing during these weeks?
qa.a: Reena is probably excited and busy with her dance class and Mitali, and may not notice that Joseph is still waiting at the swings.

grounding: Shows a boy left behind by a drifting friend, wondering what he did, when the real cause is her new dance class and new company.

passage:
Your Dadu will tell you something, beta. When I was eleven, in Nashik, my best friend was Madhav. Every evening in January we flew kites from his terrace, shouting till our mothers called us down.
Then Madhav joined an evening tuition, and after that the colony cricket team. First he came up to the terrace every day, then twice a week, then not at all. Nobody fought. Nobody said anything.
I was sure I must have done something. I remembered the time I tore his best kite and wondered if he'd been angry all along. Every evening at five I felt a heavy, dull feeling in my stomach.
Years later, at a wedding, I asked him. He blinked. "Darshan? You? I was just so tired from tuition, yaar. I thought you'd found new friends."
So when your friend stops calling, don't decide too quickly that it's you.

qa.q: Where did Darshan and Madhav fly kites every evening in January?
qa.a: They flew kites from Madhav's terrace every evening in January.

qa.q: Why did Darshan feel heavy every evening at five?
qa.a: Darshan missed Madhav and was sure he had done something wrong, even wondering if the torn kite had made Madhav angry all along.

qa.q: What turning point does Darshan want the grandchild to take from this?
qa.a: Not to decide too quickly that a fading friend is rejecting you; asking gently, or waiting before blaming yourself, can show the real reason.

qa.q: How did Madhav see the same months?
qa.a: Madhav was just tired from tuition and busy with cricket, and even thought Darshan had found new friends, so there was no rejection on his side.

grounding: Illustrates a boy left behind by a fading friendship who assumes he did something wrong, when the real cause was his friend's busier days.

passage:
Madhav waited by the colony gate at five, the way he had every evening since Class 2, with the carrom striker in his pocket.

Farida came out at ten past, but she was with two girls from her dance class, and she only waved. "Can't today, Madhav! Practice!"

It was the fourth time that week.

He went up the stairs slowly. At dinner he pushed his dal around and asked his mother, "Did I do something to Farida?"

"Did you fight?"

"No." That was the strange part. There had been no fight. She still smiled at him in the lift. She just wasn't there anymore.

That night he lay awake going through every day of the last month, looking for the thing he had done wrong, and not finding it.

qa.q: What did Madhav carry in his pocket to the colony gate?
qa.a: The carrom striker.

qa.q: Why does Madhav lie awake going through the last month?
qa.a: He feels a dull hurt and confusion, wondering what he did wrong, because there was no fight to explain why Farida drifted away.

qa.q: What could Madhav's mother say that might help him?
qa.a: She could explain that friends sometimes get busy with new things like dance class, and that it may not be about anything he did; she could also help him ask Farida gently.

qa.q: How might Farida see these evenings?
qa.a: She is probably just busy and excited about dance practice and her new friends, and may not realise how much Madhav is missing her.

grounding: Madhav feels a dull ache and wonders what he did when Farida drifts toward her dance friends, although the real cause is new company and a busier schedule.

passage:
"Chechi, does Stephen hate me?"

"Why would he hate you, Jomon?"

"He doesn't sit with me on the bus now. He sits with the chess boys."

"Did you ask him why?"

"No! Then he'll know I care."

"Hmm. Did you fight?"

"No. That's the thing. He still says hi."

"So he says hi, but you don't go to his house anymore?"

"He has chess club on Saturdays now. And tuition on Sundays."

Payal put her book down. "Jomon, that sounds like a very busy boy. Not a boy who hates you."

"Then why do I feel like this?"

"Like what?"

"Like... heavy. Here." He pressed his chest.

"That's missing someone. It's allowed."

"But I didn't even lose him properly."

"Sometimes that's the hardest kind."

qa.q: Who does Stephen sit with on the bus now?
qa.a: He sits with the chess boys.

qa.q: What does Jomon pressing his chest and saying he feels "heavy" suggest?
qa.a: It suggests he feels a dull ache of sadness and missing Stephen, mixed with a worry that he has been rejected.

qa.q: What does Payal do well in this conversation?
qa.a: She helps Jomon see that Stephen is busy rather than hateful, and she tells him that missing someone is allowed, without dismissing his feeling.

qa.q: Why might Stephen not realise Jomon is hurt?
qa.a: Stephen still says hi and is busy with chess club and tuition, so he may think nothing has changed between them.

grounding: Jomon, left behind by a friend who joined chess club, feels a heavy ache and assumes rejection, while his sister helps him see it is busier days and new company.

passage:
Last year Vidya and I did everything together. We shared a bench, we shared a water bottle, we had a handshake with four parts.

This year she got into the school choir. At first I waited outside the music room after school. Then the choir started staying late, and I started walking home alone.

Nobody said anything. She never said "I don't want to be your friend." She just wasn't at the gate anymore, and when I sent her a message about the handshake, she replied with a thumbs up, nothing else.

For weeks I thought I had done something. Maybe I talked too much. Maybe she thought my jokes were babyish.

Then my cousin said, "Pema, choir kids practise every day. She's just tired." I don't know if that's all it is. It still hurts a bit.

qa.q: What did Vidya join this year?
qa.a: The school choir.

qa.q: How does Pema feel about Vidya's thumbs-up reply?
qa.a: Pema feels hurt and uncertain, reading the short reply as a sign of rejection and wondering if the jokes were too babyish.

qa.q: What small step could help Pema at this stage?
qa.a: Pema could ask Vidya directly and kindly whether choir keeps her busy, instead of guessing, or find another time to meet, like a weekend.

qa.q: What would change if Vidya had explained that choir practice ran late every day?
qa.a: Pema might still miss her but would not feel rejected, since the drift would have a clear reason that wasn't about Pema.

grounding: Pema feels a quiet hurt and assumes rejection as Vidya drifts to choir, although the likely cause is busier days, not dislike.

passage:
Class 4 teacher's note, Friday.

Jagdish has been quiet this week. At lunch he sits on the steps near the library with his tiffin, watching the chess club by the window. Until last month, he and Nitin were always together at recess, building forts out of benches.

Nitin joined the chess club three weeks ago. He's there every lunch now with four new friends. I asked him about Jagdish; he looked puzzled and said, "We're still friends. I'm just busy."

Today Jagdish asked me, very softly, "Ma'am, did I do something bad to Nitin?" His eyes were wet.

I told him I didn't think so, that sometimes people get busy with new things. I suggested he ask Nitin to play on Saturday. I'll also mention the chess club to Jagdish; he might like it.

qa.q: What club did Nitin join?
qa.a: Nitin joined the chess club.

qa.q: What was Jagdish feeling when he asked if he'd done something bad?
qa.a: He felt hurt and confused, a dull ache of being left behind, and assumed the drift was his fault.

qa.q: How can the teacher help Jagdish now?
qa.a: By gently explaining the drift isn't rejection, encouraging a Saturday invite to Nitin, and helping Jagdish find his own new activity.

qa.q: How does Nitin see the change in their friendship?
qa.a: Nitin doesn't see it as a change at all; he feels they are still friends and is simply busy with new company.

grounding: A teacher sees a child left behind by a busy friend assume he did something wrong, when the drift comes only from new activities.
